title: Sort an Array (Merge Sort)
description: Brute force to optimized: selection sort versus merge sort, the classic O(n log n) divide-and-conquer algorithm.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array of integers nums, sort it in ascending order and return it, without using any built-in sorting function.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.text: The task is to reorder nums into ascending order. Since a simple O(n squared) sort would be too slow at 5*10^4 elements, an O(n log n) divide-and-conquer sort (merge sort) is the expected approach: split the array in half, recursively sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves back together.

blocks.title: Analogy: Merging Two Sorted Piles of Sorted Cards
blocks.text: Picture splitting a deck of cards in half, having someone else sort each half independently, and then merging the two already-sorted piles back together by repeatedly taking the smaller of the two piles' top cards, this merge step is fast and simple once both piles are individually sorted.

blocks.caption: Merge sort divides in half recursively, then merges sorted halves back together

blocks.text: Before considering simple comparison-swap sorts (which cost O(n squared)), notice that if two halves of the array were ALREADY sorted, merging them into one fully sorted array takes only O(n) using a two-pointer sweep, which is exactly what enables an O(n log n) divide-and-conquer sort.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Sorting the whole array can be broken into sorting its left half, sorting its right half, and then MERGING the two sorted halves, a classic divide-and-conquer decomposition.

Observation 2: The merge step, given two already-sorted sequences, can produce a single sorted sequence in O(n) by repeatedly comparing the fronts of each sequence and taking the smaller one.

Observation 3: Recursively applying this same divide-and-merge process down to single-element subarrays (which are trivially "sorted") builds the full sort from the bottom up.

Observation 4: Since the array is halved at each recursive level (O(log n) levels), and each level does O(n) total work merging, the overall time complexity is O(n log n).
This leads to merge sort: recursively split the array in half, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves using a two-pointer sweep, giving O(n log n) overall.
Use a simple comparison-based sort like selection sort: repeatedly find the minimum of the remaining unsorted portion and swap it into place.

items: For each position i from left to right, find the index of the minimum value among positions i to the end.
Swap that minimum value into position i.
Repeat until the whole array is sorted.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Selection sort directly implements "find the minimum, place it, repeat," which is simple and correct.
It does O(n) work to find the minimum at EVERY one of the n positions, giving O(n squared) total, too slow for n up to 5*10^4.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), scanning for the minimum at every position.
Space: O(1) extra (in-place).
Limitation: O(n squared) is too slow for n up to 5*10^4 (2.5 billion operations); merge sort achieves O(n log n) by exploiting that merging two already-sorted halves is fast.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why comparison-swap sorts are limited: any sort that only compares and swaps ADJACENT or nearby elements needs many passes to move an element far from its correct position, costing O(n squared) in the worst case.

The divide-and-conquer insight: instead of sorting the WHOLE array directly, sort two HALVES independently (recursively, down to single elements which are trivially sorted), then merge them.

Why merging is fast: given two sorted sequences, a two-pointer sweep comparing their fronts and always taking the smaller one produces the fully sorted combination in exactly O(length of both sequences combined).

The core idea: recursively divide, then merge, giving O(log n) levels of recursion each doing O(n) total merge work, for O(n log n) overall.
Recursively split nums into two halves, sort each half, then merge the two sorted halves using a two-pointer sweep into a temporary array, copying it back into the original range.

blocks.caption: Merge sort: divide recursively to single elements, merge sorted halves back together

blocks.text: Recursively splitting down to single elements (trivially sorted) and merging back up guarantees that every merge step combines two already-correctly-sorted sequences. The two-pointer merge correctly interleaves them in ascending order in O(combined length) time, and since there are O(log n) levels of recursion, each contributing O(n) total merge work across all its subarrays, the overall time is O(n log n).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), O(log n) recursive levels each doing O(n) total merge work.
Space: O(n) for the temporary merge arrays (plus O(log n) recursion stack).

blocks.text: Sort an Array is the canonical introduction to merge sort, the quintessential divide-and-conquer algorithm: divide until trivial, then merge sorted results back together in linear time per level.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "sort without a built-in function, at scale", think: merge sort, divide and conquer with an O(n) merge step.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Selection sort runs in O(n squared) time and O(1) space; merge sort runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space, making it the practical choice for large inputs.

items: Pattern: merge sort, the canonical divide-and-conquer sorting algorithm.
Core Idea: recursively split in half down to single elements, then merge sorted halves back together using a two-pointer sweep.
Time: O(n squared) for selection sort, O(n log n) for merge sort.
Most Important Observation: merging two already-sorted sequences takes only linear time, which is what makes the divide-and-conquer decomposition pay off.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational algorithm every engineer should be able to implement from memory.
One line memory trick: split in half, sort each half, merge with two pointers.
